stem: A trust fund is to be set up today to pay an annual scholarship of Rs 18000 starting exactly one year from now in perpetuity. The fund earns 9% per annum on the first Rs 100000 and 12% per annum on any balance above Rs 100000. Both rates are compounded annually. What is the minimum amount that must be deposited today to sustain the scholarship forever?

per_option_rationale.rationale: Using a single flat rate of 9% for the entire principal: P = 18000/0.09 = 200000, ignoring the tiered structure.
Using a single flat rate of 12% throughout: P = 18000/0.12 = 150000, ignoring the lower rate on the first Rs 100000.
Setting only 0.12 * (P - 100000) = 18000, ignoring the 9% earned on the first tier: P - 100000 = 150000, so P = 166667, which does not account for the Rs 9000 from the first tier.

explanation: For a perpetuity the fund must earn exactly the annual payment each year without depleting capital. With a tiered rate, the total annual income is 9% on Rs 100000 plus 12% on the excess. Setting income equal to Rs 18000 and solving gives P = Rs 175000. This is an L3 item because the perpetuity formula (PMT/r) must be adapted to a piecewise rate structure, requiring the solver to decompose the income into two tiers and form an equation in P.

explanation_sections.punchline: A tiered-rate perpetuity requires writing income as a piecewise sum and solving for the break-even principal, not simply applying PMT/r to one rate.
explanation_sections.approach: Name the formula: for a perpetuity, annual income = P for the fund to be self-sustaining. Decompose income: 0.09 * 100000 + 0.12 * (P - 100000) = 18000. Expand: 9000 + 0.12P - 12000 = 18000. Simplify: 0.12P = 21000. Solve: P = 175000.
explanation_sections.lesson: When rates are tiered, the simple PMT/r formula gives the wrong answer; always model the income in pieces and sum them before equating to the required payment.
explanation_sections.timing: 100-120 seconds. The hidden step is recognising the tiered income structure. Trap: using a single rate (9% gives 200000, 12% gives 150000); another trap is computing only the marginal tier income.
